name: The republican doctrine of the Discourses: checks and balances and the value of liberty
plain_explanation: In his longer, more sincere work, Machiavelli argues for constitutions that balance the power of prince, nobles, and people against each other, praises Sparta's constitution (as more balanced than Athens's), values the Roman republic's conflict of Senate and people, and argues -- against most classical authors -- that the common people are generally wiser and more constant than princes.
precise_definition: Russell's account of the Discourses' 'doctrine of checks and balances... set forth explicitly': 'Princes, nobles, and people should all have a part in the Constitution... then these three powers will keep each other reciprocally in check,' with a stated preference for popular government grounded not in natural rights but in the empirical observation that popular governments are 'less cruel, unscrupulous, and inconstant than tyrannies.'
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as at least as important as the more famous 'immoral' doctrines of The Prince, and as a direct historical channel through which classical republican political thought (largely dormant since antiquity) was transmitted to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
historical_origin: Modeled on Livy's history of the Roman Republic and on the constitutions of Sparta (Lycurgus) and Athens (Solon).
examples: Praise of the Spartan constitution of Lycurgus as more balanced than Solon's more democratic Athenian constitution
Praise of the Roman republican constitution's built-in conflict between Senate and people
competing_positions: Livy's and most other classical writers' view that princes are wiser and more constant than the people, which Machiavelli explicitly rejects
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes its resemblance to Montesquieu and its readability by 'an eighteenth-century liberal,' directly linking Machiavelli to the later theory of separation of powers.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Machiavelli treats religion instrumentally, as valuable for its social-cementing effect (citing Roman use of auguries) rather than for its truth.
